content.text: Mapped the structure: motor rules map a binary decision onto button pairs (M1→0/2, M3→3/2 share a button). Now searching for dissociating test tasks.
Baselines vary a lot by task (L4-S2-M3 is intrinsically easy), so checking a few more before choosing the design.
Baselines collected (L2-S1-M1 ≈ 49, L1-S1-M3 ≈ 48). Now training on L1-S1-M1.
Early signal: L1-S1-M3 (similar mapping) got faster, L2-S1-M1 (shares 2 rules but 0% overlap) didn't. Noise is high, so collecting more samples.
Interesting conflict: L1-S1-M4 (0% overlap, but only a new motor rule) also looks faster. A new logic rule might just cost more under part-based, so I'm comparing within the motor dimension.
Data are in and consistently follow mapping similarity rather than the count of new rules. Submitting.

L2-S1-M1 (1 new rule, 0 overlap) stayed at about 48 (baseline 49). L1-S1-M4 (1 new motor rule, 0 overlap) averaged about 34 (baseline about 39, small change). L1-S2-M3 (2 new rules, 0.56 overlap) averaged about 24, faster than both 1-new-rule tasks with 0 overlap, which is the opposite of the part-based prediction. Within the motor dimension, M3 (similar) transferred much better than M4 (dissimilar), which rules out an explanation based on different costs per dimension. Tests are noisy (SD about 15), so confidence is moderate."}'

content.text:
I submitted **holistic** with 0.85 confidence, using 41 of the 60 budget.

**Design:** I first tested several tasks on the untrained learner to get a baseline for how hard each one is on its own. Then I trained it on only one task, L1-S1-M1, and retested. The retested tasks were picked to pull the two hypotheses apart: some share two of the three rules with the trained task but have very different input-output mappings, and others have more new rules but similar mappings.

| Test task | New rules | Overlap with trained task | Examples needed after training (mean) | Untrained baseline |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| L1-S1-M3 | 1 | 0.75 | ~18 | ~48 |
| L1-S2-M3 | 2 | 0.56 | ~24 | — |
| L1-S1-M4 | 1 | 0 | ~34 | ~39 |
| L2-S1-M1 | 1 | 0 | ~48 | ~49 |
| L4-S4-M4 | 3 | 0 | 61 (one test) | 41 (one test) |

**Why holistic:**
- **Order of the results:** the speed-up follows how similar the mappings are, not how many rules are new.
- **Key comparison:** L1-S2-M3 has two new rules but was faster than both tasks with only one new rule and no overlap. A part-based learner should do the opposite.
- **Ruling out an alternative:** a part-based learner might find a new logic rule harder to learn than a new motor rule. To rule that out, I compared two tasks that differ only in the motor rule. The one with a similar mapping (M3) improved a lot; the one with no overlap (M4) barely changed.

**Caveats:**
- **Noise:** a single test of the same task ranged from 1 to 69 examples (spread of about ±15), so I used 4 to 8 tests per key task.
- **Lopsided tasks:** tasks that give the same answer on most inputs are easy even untrained. L4-S2-M3 took only 3–11 examples, so I left tasks like that out of the comparisons.
- **Confidence:** the pattern was consistent throughout, but with this much noise I kept confidence at 0.85.
